summary: Top Traders Unplugged episode (Aug 2026) on markets as complex adaptive systems. Dredge (convexity/options) and Brennan (trend) argue for non-ergodic, fat-tailed thinking: calm builds risk, leverage and price-insensitive flows drive moves, Sharpe/Kelly/VaR mislead. Prescriptions: add convexity, cap leverage, equal-risk sizing, widen the book, enter small.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my trend barometer yesterday finished at 45 which is pretty neutral
claims.claim: Late-July 2026 data point: trend barometer 45 (neutral); SG CTA +8.5% YTD, SG Trend +8.3%, short-term traders index +3.34% YTD, so slower trend beat short-term trend.
claims.indicator: trend barometer; SG Trend and Short-Term Traders indices

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: The two times levered ETF is down 47%.
claims.claim: Daily-rebalanced 2x levered ETFs suffer volatility drag: SK Hynix ETF fell 47% over three months while the stock ended +1% after a +125% peak, so over long horizons levered ETFs approach zero.
claims.direction: avoid long-term holding of daily levered ETFs

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: multi-year, multi-deade highs in longdated bond yields in Japan, in the US, in Britain.
claims.claim: July 2026: multi-decade highs in long-dated yields in Japan, US and UK, Fed holding with three dissents and bond-market disappointment.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Both of you see markets as complex adapted systems rather than as statistical distributions to be sampled and estimated.
claims.claim: Framing: Dredge (options/convexity) and Brennan (trend following) both treat markets as complex adaptive systems, so Gaussian statistics are the wrong mathematics and risk is not volatility.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: It's about making your car as resilient as it can possibly be and then being able to react and respond to the unknowable path of
claims.claim: Because the future path is unknowable (infinite paths around a strange attractor), investors should understand current initial conditions and build resilience (brakes) rather than forecast.
claims.direction: buy protection and keep ability to react

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: it's a world of of uh reflexivity you know where you know matter tells space how to curve and space tells matter how to move
claims.claim: Markets are reflexive, non-stationary, computationally irreducible processes where agents react to a system that reacts to them, so outcomes cannot be forecast with linear statistics (Mandelbrot: roughness at every scale).

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: there is very little evidence that anyone has significantly beaten the market. Uh, the market is the master.
claims.claim: Brennan claims little evidence that anyone has beaten the market despite clever quants, because inappropriate (Gaussian) mathematics is applied to a reflexive domain.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: positioning is the only thing that matters.
claims.claim: Dredge's dictum: positioning (especially price-insensitive flow) is what moves markets; he splits participants into 'rational accounting man' (price-insensitive, rule/regulation-driven: banks, pensions, insurers, central banks, FX reserve managers, passive) and boundedly rational agents with skin in the game.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: the bond market went well through that at the peak of what I call the mother of all bubbles of bond markets
claims.claim: The bond market is the biggest price-insensitive imbalance; holders (central banks, FX reserves, banks, pensions/insurers) sit on massive unrealised losses without cutting positions, because they do not mark to market, so the unwind of the 2020 bond bubble is incomplete.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: The lack of capital is the strange attractor at times pulling the market that direction because of the proliferation of loss management as that leverage has to get cleansed from the system.
claims.claim: Leverage is the risk (left-skewed returns, fat tails); when regulators measure risk as volatility, low vol licenses leverage, imbalances build reflexively and unwind violently as loss-absorbing capital is depleted.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the transaction event that moves price.
claims.claim: Price moves because of transactions; fundamentals, macro and flows are downstream, and an ecosystem of participant types (fundamental, trend, convergent, random) applies directed forces whose feedback creates fractal price structure.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Um uh no fat tails, no memory, no volatility clustering. Um it was exactly what you you the outcomes you'd expect from the efficient market hypothesis
claims.claim: Agent-based model with only random traders gives Gaussian returns with no fat tails, memory or volatility clustering.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: about 25% and above of participants that are divergent. Um all of the signatures you see in the real market automatically come back into the market.
claims.claim: At roughly 25% divergent (amplifying) participants, fat tails, volatility clustering and memory appear; passive investing counts as divergent because it follows a rule to buy the biggest.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: It was a transition event.
claims.claim: The simulation shows a sharp phase transition at about 25% divergent participation rather than a gradual change, so amplifying positions create the tails, memory and volatility clusters seen in real markets.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: people because they're following very simplified rules of gaussian linearity uh erotic single slices of time they are taking more risk than they have the loss appetite for
claims.claim: Big moves come from lack of loss-absorbing capital plus unstable correlation assumptions: when correlation misbehaves, investors must cut risk, which changes correlation for the next investor and triggers divergent traders, a reflexive chain.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: most people do a pretty good job of managing the risk they manage or managing the risk they measure. But what they don't do a very good job of is managing the risk they assume, the risk they don't measure.
claims.claim: Portfolio risk missed is mostly correlation and volatility assumed constant in MPT/EMH frameworks; implicit leverage via volatility selling creates mispriced tails.
claims.testable: yes - compare realised vs assumed correlation

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: it was 90% of the moves were from indogenous sources
claims.claim: Citing Bouchaud, about 90% of big market moves come from endogenous sources, not news; activity picks up, liquidity thins, the book fragilises, then a trigger hits and settling takes longer than the orthodoxy assumes.
claims.indicator: news vs price move correlation; liquidity thinning

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: calm begets calm
claims.claim: Volatility clusters, so calm periods can persist while risk accumulates in the structure; the transition from calm to volatile catches everyone.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: a 50% draw down isn't corrected with a 50% recovery. You're not back. You got to get a 100% recovery to get back.
claims.claim: Investing is non-ergodic: the ensemble average does not equal the time average (geometric vs arithmetic mean), sequencing matters, and ruin ends the game (Peters, Taleb).

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: all of the standard metrics sharp sortino variance at risk standard deviation they all stayed the same but what did change was the wealth
claims.claim: Reshuffling 40 years of identical returns left Sharpe, Sortino, VaR and standard deviation unchanged but terminal wealth ranged from a 30% decline to an 84% decline, so order-dependent path matters and these metrics miss it.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: as volatility increases as Dave talks about volatility drag you find that that difference increases in a compounded manner.
claims.claim: Volatility drag widens the gap between geometric and arithmetic paths in a compounding way, so wealth is a multiplicative process and arithmetic returns mislead.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: the fire risk grows as the forest goes longer and longer without a fire because you get more clogged brush between the trees.
claims.claim: Self-organised criticality: risk grows the longer there is no fire; diversification protects against a lightning strike on one tree but not against fire spreading through connectivity (leverage, correlation), as in a percolation threshold or an avalanche triggered by one snowflake.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: things like value at risk are measuring the frequency, a short-term frequency of past fires. And it says, well, there hasn't been a fire, so there's no risk.
claims.claim: VaR measures the frequency of past fires, so protection (options) is cheapest exactly where risk is highest, after long calm and price-insensitive supply; that is his secret sauce, e.g. rising debt/GDP without a blow-up is more reason to worry.
claims.indicator: VaR / realised volatility versus option price
claims.direction: buy tail protection when realised vol is low

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: Markets are not closed systems that equilibrate. Um they're open systems
claims.claim: Calm markets are not equilibrium; quiet is energy building like a stretched rubber band that traditional risk metrics hide.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: they are the deepest coupled negative feedback states in the entire data set.
claims.claim: In his research quiet markets are the deepest coupled negative-feedback states (oscillations cancelling), and most risk events emerge from calm regimes via a volatility shock, not from already volatile regimes.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: They will have a period of calm and their models mechanistically increase the position size in that period of calm because they're saying it's a safe market.
claims.claim: Volatility-targeted sizing mechanically raises positions in calm and behavioural leverage-up adds to it; Japanese government bonds in 2018 had 9% trailing vol authorising 16.4x leverage, so a 6% move cost 9% of capital.
claims.direction: cap leverage, do not equate calm with safety
claims.testable: yes - vol-target backtests around vol shocks

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: A high sharp ratio well that's actually authorizing a higher leverage and uh that's exactly what you don't want to be doing.
claims.claim: High Sharpe ratios authorise more leverage, which is dangerous because the estimates are noisy and tails fat.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: you want to own and invest in things with thin tails, things that have high natural
claims.claim: Own assets with thin tails and high natural volatility, and build hedges from things with artificially suppressed volatility and attracted leverage (bank/repo leverage, volatility selling), which have fat left tails; trend followers need only a few fat-tail winners with small losses (e.g. cocoa).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the whole secret that trend followers brought to the table back in the 70s is that they understood how to manage the risk and they understood how to size positions
claims.claim: Niels argues the real trend-following edge is risk management and position sizing rather than breakout signals.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the problem of being optimal is that it foregoes the room for being wrong.
claims.claim: Kelly-optimal sizing sits at a peak where overbetting quickly causes ruin, assumes perfect information, and uses estimates whose required sample explodes with fat tails; under-betting gives room for error.
claims.testable: yes - simulate fractional vs Kelly under estimation noise

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: it outperforms the the the Kelly approach when you start introducing things such as regime changes sufficient noise to your estimate
claims.claim: His tests show simple equal-risk fractional sizing outperforms Kelly-based sizing once regime changes and estimation noise are included, because noise often exceeds the signal; LTCM exceeded the peak assumptions and went to ruin.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: the two percentiles of returns, the 10 worst months out of 480 months and the 10 best months out of 480 months contribute almost all of the returns.
claims.claim: The S&P 500's 10 worst and 10 best months of 480 contribute almost all long-term returns, so the average is meaningless and what happens in the tails (penalty boxes) matters.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: the convex goalkeeper theorem
claims.claim: World Cup study: tournaments in a non-ergodic knockout are won by defensive resilience near own box, then attacking efficiency near the opponent's box, then individual tail events; used as an analogy for convex portfolio construction.
claims.testable: partly - sports data analogy, not a market test

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: They did what is so common in the investment industry. They thought they could reduce risk by capping the upside.
claims.claim: Parking the bus is like a covered call or 60/40: capping upside does not remove tail exposure; you must be convex on both sides where it matters.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: October 2008, that was a fantastic period for trend followers. It was the single largest month in the return for the entire history of 40 years that that um I looked at.
claims.claim: October 2008 was 3.4% of total trend-portfolio wealth over 40 years yet the Sharpe ratio moved only from 914 to 931 (2 cents in the dollar), so Sharpe penalises convex strategies.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: consider two portfolios both with a a sharp ratio of 1.5.
claims.claim: Two portfolios with identical Sharpe 1.5 (one concentrated Kelly bet, one wide book of small loosely related positions) differ in failure modes; Sharpe discards construction, so architecture and dependencies must be assessed.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: Yes, sometimes right just not when it matters the most right.
claims.claim: Traditional diversification assumes stable correlation and ignores connectivity; diversification across things that can each lose everything is bad, whereas diversification across positions with unbounded upside (St. Petersburg paradox) is good.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I think that markets are always permanently coupled.
claims.claim: Markets are permanently coupled via multi-product diversified agents; in calm regimes the coupling oscillates and cancels (apparent diversification) but in crisis it turns into trend and everything correlates; diversification must be judged by architecture (e.g. borrow short/lend long across a dozen markets is one rate bet).

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: with increased diversification we get an initial drop in curtosis and then a ramping up of curtasis
claims.claim: With fractal structure, greater diversification gives an initial drop in kurtosis then rising kurtosis, so more markets give more exposure to right-tail events (e.g. cocoa) rather than diluting tails.
claims.indicator: portfolio kurtosis vs number of markets

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the major material moves, the tail properties that Dave um is convincing us about, and I totally agree with him, they are the major drivers.
claims.claim: Using 125 years of Dow and S&P data, major moves hold the information and the rest is noise; larger samples expose bigger fractal structures, so drawdowns and returns ahead are larger than those seen.
claims.indicator: 125 years of Dow Jones and S&P 500 data

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: I'm creating the trend following type benefit for our investors as opposed to running it ourself.
claims.claim: Convex Strategies frees clients' capital from poor diversifiers into explicit negative-correlation hedges so clients keep positive drift assets and the combination provides long gamma on the combined portfolio.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: we're buying longdated term periods of the missed pricing of the underlying distribution which itself is driven by the supply of volatility dominated by non-prics sensitive participants
claims.claim: Long-dated options are mispriced because volatility supply is dominated by price-insensitive structured-product sellers; buying a multi-year strip at a fixed price captures a triple mispricing (distribution, supply, product nonlinearity) and the seller may want to unwind after one tail.
claims.conditions: where structured product supply depresses prices

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: when you're positively convex, more risk is less risk.
claims.claim: When positively convex, additional risk reduces total risk; the price of convexity is driven by non-price-sensitive participants; opposing views are welcome as convexity can be bought on either side.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: truncate that left tail as we do it with our stops. We do it with our small bets.
claims.claim: Trend following and long options both truncate the left tail and leave the right tail open; stop-loss longs are synthetic calls; trend followers pay an implicit premium via whipsaws and foregone growth, with gap risk that options avoid.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: Every way you can add convexity add convexity.
claims.claim: Long volatility and trend are complementary (different distribution parts and attachment points; trend has wider market breadth, options need efficient vol markets); combining them improves convexity.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: if you add the S&P and you know 50% 50% on capital, uh it's not just the average, it's almost the sum of the two.
claims.claim: A 50/50 mix of S&P 500 and trend following (or long vol) yields almost the sum of the returns rather than the average because the correlation is negative in crises.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: Expected return is a nonsensical number and it's destroyed more wealth for capital owners than maybe any other simple thing.
claims.claim: Fiduciary incentives should shift from calendar-year arithmetic returns to geometric wealth growth; do not optimise to a backward-looking expectation but build resilience by learning by doing.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: cap leverage in absolute terms
claims.claim: Cap leverage in absolute terms to break the automatic link between a quiet market and a large position, since most capital destruction comes from too much leverage in quiet markets.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: size every market with the same risk rather than tilting towards whichever edge looks currently strongest
claims.claim: Size every market to equal risk instead of tilting to the apparently strongest edge, because edge differences are smaller than estimation noise and tilting rebuilds a single cable and misses cocoa-like explosions.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: grow by widening the book, not by scaling the bets.
claims.claim: Grow return by adding unrelated systems/markets rather than scaling existing bets; and enter small, letting open profit build the position.
claims.direction: add breadth, pyramid from open profit

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: most people are levering concave risks.
claims.claim: Leverage on concave positions (low correlation in good markets, rising in bad) creates volatility drag and disasters; adding non-recourse leverage in the form of options on convex hedges is risk-reducing, enabling portable alpha / return stacking with trend or long vol.
claims.direction: add convex overlay then take more equity risk

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: I'm 100% trend so I never have to face this demon
claims.claim: Brennan views long-vol overlays on traditional portfolios as a band-aid; ideally rebuild the portfolio from first principles.

claims.speaker: Dave Dredge (CIO Convex Strategies, options/convexity)
claims.quote: risk is about accountability
claims.claim: Dredge's closing view: risk is managed by accountability and tacit knowledge, not by magic models; embedding VaR in BIS capital rules removed accountability and invited the GFC.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: risk is everything you didn't think of
claims.claim: Risk is everything not in your backtest.
